claims.text: The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy has a disordered solid-solution microstructure without intentional secondary phases.
Adding a minor amount of yttrium and applying controlled oxidation will form nanoscale Y2O3 particles in the alloy.
The resulting Y2O3 particles will be homogeneously distributed in the alloy matrix.
The nanoscale Y2O3 particles will remain thermally stable within the alloy matrix.
Y2O3 particles will impede dislocation motion under high-temperature loading.
Impeded dislocation motion will provide dispersion strengthening at high temperature.
Y2O3 particles will act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Defect-sink activity will mitigate the accumulation of irradiation-induced defects.
The Y2O3 dispersion will maintain the overall phase stability of the alloy under thermal and irradiation exposure.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength than the same alloy without the oxide dispersion.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will better tolerate irradiation-induced damage than the same alloy without the oxide dispersion.
The predicted benefits will hold around 1000–1200 degrees Celsius under ion irradiation that simulates reactor exposure.
Particle coarsening or agglomeration could reduce or eliminate the strengthening and irradiation-tolerance benefits.
Formation of undesirable intermetallic phases could reduce or eliminate the proposed benefits.
